name: Coast Redwood (Sequoia sempervirens)
where: Alluvial flats along the Smith River and its forks (Stout Grove, Simpson-Reed Grove, Grove of Titans) — the flat, silty ground floods regularly and feeds the biggest trees; smaller on drier slopes and ridges.
idMarks: Very tall, straight trunk with thick, deeply-furrowed fibrous reddish-brown bark that feels spongy and fire-resistant; flat, short needles (two ranks on shade branches, awl-like on sun branches near the crown); small egg-shaped cones about the size of a grape/olive. Often has a fire-hollowed 'goosepen' at the base and burl sprouts around it.
season: Evergreen year-round; best light for photos is midday when fog burns off in the groves.
funFact: Coast redwoods are the tallest living trees on Earth; many of the tallest known individuals grow in nearby Redwood Creek and Prairie Creek groves, and the 'Grove of Titans' boardwalk in Jedediah Smith opened in 2022 to protect root zones of ancient specimens.

name: Sitka Spruce (Picea sitchensis)
where: Wetter, foggier ground near the coast and along the lower Smith River where salt air reaches; less common deep in the Jed Smith groves than at Prairie Creek or the coast.
idMarks: Bark in irregular loose, scaly plates (not fibrous like redwood); needles are stiff, sharp, and flattened, arranged all around the twig ('ouch when you grab a branch' test); large papery cones with wavy-edged scales hang down from branch tips.
season: Evergreen; new spring growth ('spruce tips') is bright yellow-green.
funFact: Sitka spruce tolerates salt-laden wind better than any other Northwest conifer, which is why it dominates the immediate coastal fog belt rather than the sheltered river flats redwoods prefer.

name: Douglas-fir (Pseudotsuga menziesii)
where: Drier slopes and ridgetops above the redwood flats, mixed-evergreen forest along Howland Hill Road and the Little Bald Hills uplands.
idMarks: Bark thick, corky, deeply furrowed dark brown-gray; flat single needles spiral around the twig (not flat two-ranked like redwood); cones hang down and have distinctive three-pronged bracts ('mouse tails and back legs') sticking out between the scales — the single best ID feature.
season: Evergreen; cones mature and drop in fall.
funFact: Despite the name it's not a true fir — the pitchfork-shaped bracts poking out of every cone are unique among Pacific Northwest conifers and instantly separate it from grand fir or hemlock.

name: Western Hemlock (Tsuga heterophylla)
where: Shady, moist slopes and older-growth understory throughout the redwood/Douglas-fir forest, often as an understory tree beneath the redwood canopy.
idMarks: Drooping, feathery leader (the very top of the tree flops over — a reliable ID at a distance); short flat needles of noticeably uneven lengths on the same twig; small cones under an inch long. Bark is thin, scaly, reddish-brown to gray.
season: Evergreen.
funFact: The floppy top makes it identifiable from far away even when the rest of the tree is hidden in the canopy — locals call it the tree that can't stand up straight.
flagReason: General regional occurrence is well established in Pacific NW old growth but I could not confirm from a fetched Jed Smith-specific source how common western hemlock is inside the park proper versus Six Rivers NF slopes.

name: Grand Fir (Abies grandis)
where: Occurs locally on moister slopes and stream terraces in the Smith River drainage, mixed with Douglas-fir and hemlock; less dominant than redwood, spruce, or Doug-fir.
idMarks: Needles flat and glossy dark green above with two white stripes below, arranged in a flat spray ('friendly fir' — soft, not prickly); bark smooth gray with resin blisters when young, furrowing with age; upright barrel-shaped cones held on top branches (fir cones disintegrate on the tree rather than falling whole).
season: Evergreen.
funFact: Grand fir needles are cut and crushed to smell like citrus/tangerine — a good field test when bark and cones aren't visible.
flagReason: Grand fir presence specifically within Jedediah Smith / lower Smith River corridor (vs. more widely in Six Rivers National Forest uplands) is a detail I could not verify from an accessible official source this session.

name: Port Orford Cedar (Chamaecyparis lawsoniana)
where: Scattered on serpentine-influenced slopes and stream drainages of the Smith River watershed, including parts of the Del Norte back-country; a species of conservation concern due to root-rot disease spread by muddy vehicle and boot traffic.
idMarks: Scale-like, flattened sprays of foliage (like a flattened arborvitae) with a white 'X' or butterfly pattern visible on the underside of the scales; small round cones about the size of a pea with shield-shaped scales; stringy fibrous reddish bark similar to redwood but the foliage is completely different.
season: Evergreen.
funFact: Because Port Orford cedar root-rot (Phytophthora lateralis) spreads in wet mud on tires and boots, this is the reason you'll see boot-cleaning stations at some regional trailheads.
safety: Do not drive or hike through muddy areas near cedar stands during wet weather without cleaning boots/tires first — this is an active regulatory concern in Six Rivers NF and Del Norte parks.
flagReason: Species is well documented regionally, but I could not confirm exact Port Orford cedar stand locations within Jed Smith SP boundaries specifically from an official source this session — treat location as approximate/regional.

name: Red Alder (Alnus rubra)
where: Riverbanks and disturbed alluvial ground along the Smith River and its gravel bars, often the first tree to colonize a fresh gravel bar after floods.
idMarks: Smooth pale gray-white bark often blotched with lichen; simple oval leaves with slightly rolled-under, toothed edges; small woody 'cones' (actually strobiles) persist on bare winter branches.
season: Deciduous — leafs out in spring, drops leaves in fall; the pale bark stands out especially in winter.
funFact: Alder roots host nitrogen-fixing bacteria, so alder groves along the river actively fertilize the gravel bars they colonize, helping later conifers establish.

name: Bigleaf Maple (Acer macrophyllum)
where: Stream banks and alluvial flats alongside redwoods, often the mossiest tree in the grove.
idMarks: Largest leaf of any maple in North America (up to 12 inches across), classic five-lobed maple shape; trunks and branches are frequently draped in thick licorice fern and moss mats, giving them a shaggy green look even in the shade of the redwood canopy.
season: Deciduous; brilliant yellow-gold fall color in October–November is one of the best fall shows in the park.
funFact: The moss and fern mats on bigleaf maple branches actually grow their own soil layer and sometimes sprout tiny 'canopy roots' from the maple to tap into it.

name: Tanoak (Notholithocarpus densiflorus)
where: Riparian flats and mixed-evergreen slopes throughout the park's understory and mid-canopy, often growing in the shade of redwoods and Douglas-fir.
idMarks: Evergreen leaves are leathery, toothed, and oak-like but the tree is not a true oak; acorns look oak-like but sit in a bristly, fringed cap unlike a smooth oak acorn cap.
season: Evergreen; acorns drop in fall and were historically an important Tolowa/Yurok food source.
funFact: Tanoak is highly vulnerable to sudden oak death (Phytophthora ramorum), a serious regional forest health concern, so dead standing tanoaks are a common and expected sight in these woods.
safety: Sudden oak death has killed large numbers of tanoaks regionally; downed/standing dead tanoak snags near trails can be a hazard tree concern after storms.
flagReason: Sudden oak death prevalence specifically in Jed Smith / Smith River corridor (vs. broader redwood region) not confirmed from a fetched park-specific source this session.

name: California Bay Laurel (Umbellularia californica)
where: Mixed forest edges, alluvial flats, and along roadsides such as Howland Hill Road.
idMarks: Glossy, narrow, pointed evergreen leaves that release a strong pungent bay/menthol smell when crushed — the single easiest tree to ID by smell in the park; small round fruits ('California bay nuts') resemble tiny avocados.
season: Evergreen; fruit ripens in fall.
funFact: Crushing a leaf and inhaling deeply can cause a brief, sharp headache in sensitive people, earning it the nickname 'headache tree.'
safety: Strong volatile oils can trigger head/sinus irritation in sensitive people if inhaled directly and repeatedly — a minor, well-known quirk rather than a real hazard.

name: Pacific Madrone (Arbutus menziesii)
where: Drier, sunnier slopes and forest edges, including along US-199 and Howland Hill Road where more light reaches the ground.
idMarks: Unmistakable smooth, thin, peeling bark that goes from green to orange-red to cinnamon and curls off in papery sheets; leathery oval evergreen leaves; clusters of small white urn-shaped flowers in spring and orange-red berries in fall.
season: Flowers in spring; berries color up in autumn; bark peels most visibly in summer heat.
funFact: Madrone berries are a favorite of band-tailed pigeons and other birds moving through in fall.

name: Pacific Rhododendron (Rhododendron macrophyllum)
where: Understory shrub throughout the redwood groves on well-drained slopes, especially visible along the Boy Scout Tree Trail and Howland Hill Road.
idMarks: Large, leathery, dark evergreen leaves; showy rose-pink to purple-pink flower clusters (trusses) held above the foliage — the park's signature spring bloom.
season: Peak bloom typically mid-May through June, varying with the year's weather.
funFact: Redwood National and State Parks' rhododendron bloom is famous enough to draw its own seasonal visitor traffic, especially along shaded stretches of Howland Hill Road.
safety: All Rhododendron parts contain grayanotoxins and are toxic if eaten; do not use the leaves or flowers for tea.
flagReason: Toxicity is well documented for the genus, flagging per safety-content rule; exact peak bloom window varies year to year and is a seasonal estimate rather than a fixed date.

name: Western Azalea (Rhododendron occidentale)
where: Understory and forest-edge shrub, often in slightly moister, more open ground than Pacific rhododendron — streambanks and grove edges.
idMarks: Deciduous (unlike rhododendron), with fragrant white-to-pale-pink flowers that have a yellow blotch on the upper petal; strong sweet fragrance is often noticeable before the flower is seen.
season: Blooms roughly May through July, generally slightly later or overlapping with rhododendron.
funFact: It's one of the most fragrant native shrubs in California — visitors often smell the bloom before they spot it.
safety: Like other Rhododendron species, all parts are toxic if ingested.
flagReason: Bloom window is a general regional estimate, not confirmed against a current-year park bloom report.

name: Salal (Gaultheria shallon)
where: Dense low understory shrub throughout the redwood forest floor and coastal scrub, especially where light gaps let it thicken up.
idMarks: Thick, waxy, oval evergreen leaves; small pink-white urn-shaped flowers in spring; dark blue-purple edible berries in summer/fall; forms nearly impenetrable thickets in places.
season: Flowers spring; berries ripen mid-to-late summer.
funFact: Salal berries were a staple food and trade item for coastal Native peoples of the Pacific Northwest, sometimes dried into cakes.
safety: Berries are edible, though often bland; no toxicity concern.

name: Evergreen Huckleberry (Vaccinium ovatum)
where: Understory shrub on slopes and forest edges throughout the redwood belt, often alongside salal.
idMarks: Small, glossy, finely-toothed evergreen leaves; small pink-white bell flowers; small dark blue-black berries in fall, smaller than a blueberry but similarly flavored.
season: Berries ripen September–November — notably later than red huckleberry.
funFact: Its late fruiting season means evergreen huckleberry can still be producing berries well into fall after most other regional berries are done.
safety: Edible and popular for jam/pie among locals.

name: Red Huckleberry (Vaccinium parvifolium)
where: Classic redwood-forest shrub, frequently rooted right on top of old stumps and downed nurse logs rather than in soil — look for it growing out of the tops of rotting redwood stumps.
idMarks: Deciduous, thin bright-green angular twigs (often greenish even in winter); small oval leaves; bright translucent red berries, tart, ripening in summer.
season: Berries ripen roughly July–August.
funFact: Because it roots so readily in decaying wood, red huckleberry is one of the best visual cues for spotting an old 'nurse stump' or nurse log in the forest.
safety: Edible, tart; used in jams.

name: Sword Fern (Polystichum munitum)
where: The single most common understory fern in the redwood groves — carpets the forest floor on slopes and flats throughout Jed Smith.
idMarks: Large, stiff, once-divided evergreen fronds standing upright in clumps; each leaflet has a small thumb-like lobe at its base near the stem, and the frond feels leathery/stiff compared to soft ferns.
season: Evergreen year-round.
funFact: NPS specifically calls out sword fern and redwood sorrel as the two most common understory plants of the redwood forest floor.

name: Redwood Sorrel (Oxalis oregana)
where: Blankets the shadiest, dampest forest floor beneath dense redwood canopy — a living green carpet in the darkest parts of the groves.
idMarks: Clover-like three-parted leaves, often with a purplish underside; small white to pink five-petaled flowers; leaves visibly fold downward ('sleep') when struck by direct sun or rain.
season: Flowers spring through summer; foliage present much of the year in shaded groves.
funFact: The leaves physically droop and fold within minutes when a sunbeam or raindrop hits them — an easy, fun thing to point out to kids on a grove walk.
safety: Contains oxalic acid like other Oxalis species — fine in small tasted amounts but not a foraging food.

name: Western Trillium (Trillium ovatum)
where: Scattered on shaded slopes and flats throughout the redwood/Douglas-fir forest floor, often near sword fern and sorrel.
idMarks: Everything comes in threes: three broad leaves in a single whorl, three petals; flower opens white and ages to pink or deep rose-purple as it matures — so a patch can show both white and pink blooms at once.
season: Blooms late winter into spring, roughly February–May depending on elevation and snowmelt.
funFact: Trillium takes years to reach flowering size from seed and is easily killed by picking (it can't easily resprout), so it's treated as a look-don't-touch wildflower everywhere in redwood country.
safety: Picking is discouraged/prohibited in state and national parkland as with all park flora; the plant itself is not toxic but is slow to recover from damage.
flagReason: General bloom timing is a regional estimate; picking-prohibition is a standard park rule but I could not re-confirm the specific regulatory citation this session.

name: Clintonia / Bead Lily (Clintonia andrewsiana)
where: Shaded, moist redwood-forest floor throughout the park, often growing near sword fern and trillium.
idMarks: A few broad, glossy basal leaves; a cluster (umbel) of pink-magenta bell-shaped flowers on a single stalk in spring, followed by a cluster of striking deep-blue berries later in the season.
season: Flowers late spring (May–June); the blue berry cluster is a late-summer highlight.
funFact: The bright cobalt-blue berry clusters that follow the flowers are one of the most photographed non-fungal details of the redwood forest floor in late summer.
safety: Berries are not considered edible/palatable for humans; not a foraging plant.

name: Five-Finger Fern (Adiantum aleuticum)
where: Moist rock faces, seeps, and streamside banks — look for it near creek crossings and wet road cuts along Howland Hill Road rather than on the dry forest floor.
idMarks: Delicate, fan-shaped fronds radiating from a shiny black-purple wiry stem, splitting into finger-like divisions — easy to tell apart from sword fern by its lacy, dark-stemmed, hand-like shape.
season: Best displayed spring through fall when seeps are still flowing.
funFact: The glossy black stem was historically used by regional Native basket weavers for pattern work, prized for its dark, durable color.

name: Deer Fern (Struthiopteris spicant / Blechnum spicant)
where: Moist shaded slopes and streambanks throughout the redwood forest, often mixed with sword fern but in wetter microsites.
idMarks: Two distinct frond types from the same plant: low, spreading, evergreen sterile fronds and separate upright, narrower, taller fertile (spore-bearing) fronds standing straight up from the center — this two-frond-type look is the key ID feature separating it from sword fern.
season: Evergreen sterile fronds year-round; fertile fronds most visible in summer.
funFact: Deer and elk are known to browse the fronds in winter when other forage is scarce, giving the fern its name.

name: California Pitcher Plant / Cobra Lily (Darlingtonia californica)
where: Confined to nutrient-poor serpentine seeps, fens, and bogs — the classic accessible viewing spot is the Darlingtonia Trail, a short boardwalk loop just off US-199 near Simpson-Reed Grove/Hiouchi, protecting a wet serpentine fen; also found in the Myrtle Creek Botanical Area (Smith River National Recreation Area) and on the serpentine barrens of the Little Bald Hills.
idMarks: Unmistakable tubular, twisted, cobra-hood-shaped leaves (yellow-green to purplish, often netted with translucent 'window' patches) that lure, trap, and digest insects; a forked, tongue-like appendage hangs from the hood mouth; yellowish-purple nodding flowers rise on separate stalks above the pitchers in late spring.
season: Flowers late spring (roughly April–June); pitchers are visible and colorful through summer.
funFact: Unlike most pitcher plants, Darlingtonia doesn't rely on digestive enzymes alone — it uses the false, light-admitting 'windows' in the hood to confuse trapped insects into repeatedly failing to find the real exit until they tire and fall in.
safety: Darlingtonia is fully protected in these serpentine seeps and easily damaged by foot traffic off the boardwalk — stay on boardwalks/trail at all viewing sites.
flagReason: Could not confirm exact lat/lng of the Darlingtonia Trail boardwalk or the precise Myrtle Creek Botanical Area / Little Bald Hills viewing points from a live official source this session (several NPS/CA Parks/Six Rivers NF URLs 404'd or lacked the detail); locations given are regionally correct but coordinates are omitted rather than guessed, and exact trail protections/regulations should be verified against a current NPS/BLM/Six Rivers NF page before publishing as fact.

name: Salmonberry (Rubus spectabilis)
where: Moist streambanks, seeps, and forest-edge thickets along the Smith River corridor, often among the first berries to ripen each year.
idMarks: Raspberry-like compound leaves in threes; thorny cane stems; bright pink-magenta flowers in early spring; soft berries ranging from salmon-orange to red, shaped like a raspberry but usually softer and more watery.
season: Flowers late winter/early spring (Feb–April); berries ripen May–June, the earliest of the local berry trio.
funFact: Salmonberry shoots were traditionally eaten peeled and raw in spring by Northwest Coast peoples, alongside the berries themselves — one of the first fresh foods of the year.
safety: Edible; no toxicity concern.

name: Thimbleberry (Rubus parviflorus)
where: Sunny forest edges, roadsides, and clearings along the Smith River corridor and Howland Hill Road, often growing in dense colonies.
idMarks: Large, soft, maple-like fuzzy leaves (no thorns on the stems, unlike salmonberry/blackberry); big white five-petaled flowers; soft, flattened, dome-shaped red berries that come off the stem hollow like a thimble.
season: Flowers late spring; berries ripen mid-to-late summer (July–August), later than salmonberry.
funFact: The berry's hollow, cap-like shape when picked — like a little thimble left on the stem — gives the plant its name.
safety: Edible, soft and seedy; a favorite trailside snack berry.

name: Red Elderberry (Sambucus racemosa)
where: Moist forest edges and streambanks along the Smith River; the confluence area was historically significant enough to Tolowa people that a village site there was named for it.
idMarks: Large compound leaves with 5–7 toothed leaflets; showy pyramidal clusters of small white flowers in spring; clusters of bright red berries in summer, held upright above the foliage (unlike the drooping dark clusters of blue elderberry).
season: Flowers April–June; berries ripen June–August.
funFact: A historic Tolowa village near the Smith River was known by a name translating to 'Red Elderberry Place,' reflecting how important the plant was to local Native foodways and place-naming.
safety: Raw red elderberry leaves, stems, and uncooked/raw berries are considered toxic/an irritant and must be cooked before any use — unlike blue elderberry, red elderberry is generally treated as not safe to eat raw.
flagReason: Could not re-confirm the exact Tolowa place-name translation/'Red Elderberry Place' village location or spelling from a live authoritative source this session (search budget exhausted before I could verify against a tribal or ethnographic source) — treat as a cultural detail needing confirmation from a Tolowa Dee-ni' Nation or ethnobotanical source before publishing, and double-check red-vs-blue elderberry raw-toxicity guidance against a poison-control-grade source.

name: Black bear (Ursus americanus)
where: Widespread through Jedediah Smith's old-growth and second-growth forest, Smith River corridor, and Del Norte County backcountry; most often seen at dawn/dusk along Howland Hill Road, Simpson-Reed Grove, and Stout Grove approaches, and occasionally near campgrounds drawn by improperly stored food.
idMarks: Uniformly black to dark brown coat (occasional cinnamon-phase individuals elsewhere in CA, less common on the coast), no shoulder hump (distinguishes from grizzly, which is extirpated from CA), flat facial profile, claw marks on big-leaf maple and red alder trunks.
season: Year-round; most active spring through fall, denning loosely in winter (coastal CA bears do not always fully hibernate given mild winters).
safety: Store all food/scented items in bear boxes or vehicles at Jed Smith and Mill Creek campgrounds; California regulations require proper food storage and prohibit feeding wildlife. Never approach; make noise on trail to avoid surprise encounters.
funFact: Coastal redwood-belt black bears will strip bark from young Douglas-fir and redwood to feed on the sugary cambium layer, a behavior foresters call 'bear damage' and actively manage for.
flagReason: General black bear ecology confirmed by long-standing NPS/CDFW consensus, but the specific park mammal page was a placeholder at fetch time — verify current NPS bear-safety specifics before publishing.

name: Roosevelt elk (Cervus canadensis roosevelti)
where: Core herds are well south of Jedediah Smith — Elk Meadow, Gold Bluffs Beach, Prairie Creek Redwoods SP, the Bald Hills, and lower Redwood Creek/Orick Valley. In Del Norte County, elk are an occasional/edge presence rather than a reliable sighting: small groups sometimes range as far north as Crescent Beach and the lower Smith River floodplain, but Jedediah Smith itself is not an elk-viewing destination.
idMarks: Largest of California's elk subspecies; bulls carry heavy, sweeping antlers shed each spring and regrown by fall for the rut; tan-brown body with pale rump patch; bugling calls audible over long distances in September-October rut.
season: Bulls bugle and herd cows Sept-Oct (rut); calves born late May-June; visible year-round at Elk Meadow/Prairie Creek but far less predictably in Del Norte.
safety: Keep 25+ yards away, especially during the fall rut when bulls are aggressive and spring when cows with calves are defensive; do not approach for photos.
funFact: Roosevelt elk are the largest-bodied elk subspecies in North America, an adaptation to the wet, browse-rich coastal temperate rainforest rather than open plains.
flagReason: NPS source confirms core herds are Crescent Beach/Gold Bluffs/Prairie Creek/Bald Hills/Orick Valley and elk range 'Freshwater Lagoon to just south of Klamath and north of Klamath near Crescent Beach' but does not explicitly confirm or deny presence at Jedediah Smith/Smith River — treat Del Norte sightings as occasional/edge-of-range, not guaranteed, and verify locally before printing as fact.

name: Black-tailed deer (Odocoileus hemionus columbianus)
where: The most commonly seen large mammal throughout Jedediah Smith — forest edges along Howland Hill Road, meadow openings, and roadside browse throughout the Smith River corridor and Crescent City outskirts.
idMarks: Smaller and darker than mule deer, black-topped tail (vs. mule deer's white tail with black tip), males grow modest forked antlers; often seen browsing ferns and shrubs at dawn/dusk.
season: Year-round; fawns born late spring, rut (bucks chasing does) in November.
safety: Common roadside collision risk on Hwy 199 and Howland Hill Road at dawn/dusk — drive slowly through the park.
funFact: This subspecies is uniquely adapted to browse the understory of dense coastal rainforest, thriving on huckleberry, salal, and sword fern that would be poor forage for open-country mule deer.

name: Mountain lion / cougar (Puma concolor)
where: Present throughout Jedediah Smith and the greater Smith River/Del Norte forest complex, following deer populations; extremely rarely seen due to solitary, crepuscular/nocturnal habits.
idMarks: Tawny/tan unspotted coat, long thick tail with dark tip, roughly house-cat-shaped head scaled up to ~150 lbs; signs include large cat tracks (no claw marks, unlike canids) and cached deer kills covered in duff.
season: Year-round resident, no seasonal pattern to sightings.
safety: California prohibits hunting mountain lions (a specially protected species since 1990) except for depredation permits; if encountered, do not run — make yourself look large, back away slowly, pick up small children.
funFact: A single mountain lion's home range can exceed 100 square miles in this rugged coastal terrain, meaning the park's entire visitor corridor is likely within one or two individual cats' territories at any time.
flagReason: General mountain lion ecology and CA protected-species status are well established, but presence specifically confirmed for Jed Smith (vs. inferred from regional range) should be checked against current park safety bulletins.

name: Bobcat (Lynx rufus)
where: Forest edges, meadows, and brushy second-growth throughout Del Norte County and along the Smith River; more often seen in open habitat than deep old growth.
idMarks: About twice house-cat size, short 'bobbed' tail with black tip on top only, spotted/streaked tawny coat, tufted ears smaller than lynx tufts.
season: Year-round; most active dawn and dusk.
safety: Not a safety concern to humans; avoid approaching if one appears with kittens.
funFact: Bobcats are excellent swimmers when needed and will cross the Smith River's gravel bars, unlike many cats' reputation for avoiding water.

name: Gray fox (Urocyon cinereoargenteus)
where: Mixed forest and brushland edges throughout the park and Smith River corridor; the only North American canid that regularly climbs trees, so it favors areas with leaning trunks and low branches.
idMarks: Grizzled gray back with rusty-orange sides and throat, black stripe down the tail to a black tip (vs. red fox's white-tipped tail); smaller and stockier than a red fox.
season: Year-round resident.
safety: None; shy and rarely approaches people.
funFact: Gray foxes have semi-retractable claws and rotating wrists, letting them scramble up leaning redwood and tanoak trunks to escape coyotes and dogs — a trick unique among American canids.

name: North American river otter (Lontra canadensis)
where: Smith River mainstem and tributaries, especially calm pools and gravel bars visible from Stout Grove access and the Hiouchi/Hwy 199 bridge; also lower stretches near the estuary.
idMarks: Long sleek brown body, thick tapered tail, travels in family groups ('romps'), frequent porpoising dives and playful slides down muddy banks.
season: Year-round; family groups with pups most visible late spring-summer.
safety: None; keep dogs leashed near riverbanks as otters can be territorial.
funFact: The Smith River's exceptional water clarity — it's one of the cleanest major rivers in California, undammed along its entire length — makes it one of the more reliable rivers in the state for daytime otter sightings.

name: Humboldt marten (Martes caurina humboldtensis)
where: A genuine old-growth rarity: this coastal marten subspecies was believed extinct until its rediscovery in 1996 in Six Rivers National Forest (which manages much of the Smith River National Recreation Area abutting Jedediah Smith). Current known populations cluster in four small patches across coastal Del Norte/Humboldt counties and the CA-OR border region — sightings within Jedediah Smith proper are not a visitor expectation.
idMarks: Weasel-family carnivore, larger and darker than a mink, rich chocolate-brown fur with an orange/cream throat patch, bushy tail; almost never seen by visitors given its rarity and dense-understory habits.
season: Year-round resident where present; no visitor viewing season exists.
safety: Federally threatened (2020) and California-endangered (2019); do not disturb if encountered, and report sightings to CDFW/USFS.
funFact: Fewer than 500 Humboldt martens survive across California and Oregon combined, split into four isolated populations — one of the rarest mammals in the entire redwood region.
flagReason: Population figure (<500) and 1996 Six Rivers NF rediscovery are from a tertiary source (Wikipedia) reflecting USFWS/CDFW findings — confirm against USFWS species profile before publishing as a precise number, and note that presence within Jedediah Smith's specific boundary (vs. the broader Six Rivers NF/Smith River NRA) is not independently confirmed.

name: Fisher (Pekania pennanti)
where: Old-growth and mature mixed-conifer forest across the Smith River drainage and Six Rivers National Forest; an old-growth specialist that depends on large snags and cavities for denning, so presence tracks the park's biggest, oldest stands.
idMarks: Larger and darker than a marten, roughly housecat-sized weasel-relative, dark brown fur, long bushy tail, low-slung loping gait; almost entirely nocturnal/crepuscular and rarely seen.
season: Year-round resident; no reliable viewing season.
safety: West Coast fisher populations are a federal candidate/protected concern in parts of their range; do not disturb.
funFact: Fishers are one of the few predators that regularly kill porcupines, flipping them onto their unspined belly in a rapid, repeated-bite attack.
flagReason: Fisher presence specifically within Del Norte/Jed Smith (vs. the broader Klamath-Siskiyou region) could not be confirmed from an official source in this pass — verify against Six Rivers NF or CDFW range maps before publishing.

name: Marbled murrelet (Brachyramphus marmoratus)
where: The signature old-growth seabird of the redwood belt — nests on wide, moss-covered branches high in ancient redwood and Douglas-fir up to 30 miles inland, including within Jedediah Smith's old-growth groves (Stout Grove, Simpson-Reed, Boy Scout Tree Trail corridor) and along the Smith River gravel bars.
idMarks: Small, chunky, dark seabird, robin-sized; the giveaway is behavioral, not visual — listen at first light for its distinctive rising, robin-like 'keer-keer' call as birds fly fast and low over the canopy between ocean feeding grounds and inland nest trees.
season: Nesting March-September, peak activity and best dawn detection mid-May through July; birds are essentially undetectable overhead once full daylight arrives.
safety: Federally threatened (1992) and California-endangered; do NOT feed jays, ravens, or squirrels anywhere in the park — food scraps inflate corvid populations, and Steller's jays are the murrelet's primary egg/chick predator, so a dropped picnic crumb has a documented causal line to nest failure a mile away.
funFact: Unlike every other North American seabird, marbled murrelets don't nest in colonies on cliffs or islands — they fly solo up to 30 miles inland to lay a single egg on a wide mossy old-growth limb, a nesting strategy not confirmed by scientists until 1974.

name: Northern spotted owl (Strix occidentalis caurina)
where: Old-growth and mature mixed-conifer stands throughout Jedediah Smith and the Smith River drainage; a genuine indicator species of unlogged forest structure, though sightings are rare and management-tracked rather than a visitor draw.
idMarks: Large dark-brown owl with white spotting (vs. barred owl's vertical brown streaking on the belly), dark eyes, rounded head with no ear tufts; call is a series of four deep hoots.
season: Year-round resident; most vocal at dusk/night in late winter-spring breeding season.
safety: Federally threatened; do not use playback calls to attract owls, which stresses breeding birds and is discouraged/restricted by land managers.
funFact: The invasive barred owl, not logging alone, is now the dominant threat to the species' survival in California — the two species compete directly and barred owls out-compete and sometimes hybridize with spotted owls, prompting active USFWS barred-owl removal programs in parts of their range.
flagReason: Population figures (roughly 560 pairs in Northern California, ~7.3%/yr decline) are regional totals from a tertiary source, not Del Norte/Jed Smith-specific — cite as range-wide context only, verify against USFWS 5-year review before quoting a precise county-level count.

name: Varied thrush (Ixoreus naevius)
where: Understory of Jedediah Smith's old-growth and shaded second-growth, especially damp fern-heavy stretches along Stout Grove and Simpson-Reed Grove trails.
idMarks: Robin-shaped but strikingly patterned: burnt-orange breast crossed by a black band, orange eyebrow stripe, slate-blue-gray back; song is an eerie single held whistled note followed by another on a different pitch, echoing through the canopy.
season: Fall through spring is when most visitors encounter them (many descend from higher-elevation breeding areas or Canada/Alaska to winter on the coast); some breed locally in deep shaded forest in summer.
safety: None.
funFact: Its haunting, buzzy single-note whistle is often the first bird sound visitors notice inside a dense redwood grove — many describe it as an almost synthesizer-like tone rather than a typical birdsong.

name: Pacific wren (Troglodytes pacificus)
where: Tangled understory and downed-log 'nurse log' habitat throughout Jedediah Smith's old growth, especially Stout Grove, Boy Scout Tree Trail, and Howland Hill Road groves.
idMarks: Tiny (4 inches), round, dark reddish-brown, stub tail cocked upward; utterly disproportionate voice — an explosive, rapid-fire cascading trill lasting several seconds, among the most complex songs of any North American bird.
season: Year-round resident; singing most persistent spring through summer.
safety: None.
funFact: Pound for pound, the Pacific wren's song is often cited as one of the most acoustically complex of any bird in North America, packing dozens of note types into a single continuous burst.

name: Steller's jay (Cyanocitta stelleri)
where: Ubiquitous throughout Jedediah Smith's forests, campgrounds, and picnic areas — the bird most visitors will actually see up close, often boldly approaching for food.
idMarks: Large, all-dark-blue-and-black jay with a tall pointed black crest; loud, harsh 'shaack-shaack-shaack' scolding call.
season: Year-round resident.
safety: Do not feed — it is illegal to feed wildlife in California state parks, and Steller's jays are the documented primary predator of marbled murrelet eggs and chicks; every dropped crumb or open food container near a campsite measurably raises local jay density and murrelet nest failure nearby.
funFact: This single, food-habituated jay is the direct ecological link between careless campground food storage and the decline of an endangered old-growth seabird a mile away in the canopy.

name: Chestnut-backed chickadee (Poecile rufescens)
where: Conifer canopy and mixed forest throughout Jedediah Smith, foraging in small mixed-species flocks with kinglets, nuthatches, and creepers.
idMarks: Small chickadee with a rich chestnut-brown back and flanks contrasting with a black cap and white cheek; call a hoarse, buzzy 'chick-a-dee' lower and raspier than other chickadees.
season: Year-round resident.
safety: None.
funFact: This is the characteristic chickadee of the humid Pacific coastal rainforest belt, largely replacing the more familiar black-capped chickadee in redwood country.

name: Brown creeper (Certhia americana)
where: Old-growth redwood and Douglas-fir trunks throughout Jedediah Smith, spiraling up bark from the base of one tree before flying down to the base of the next.
idMarks: Small, streaky brown-and-white, cryptically camouflaged against bark; thin downcurved bill and stiff tail used as a prop, woodpecker-style; song a very high thin series of notes easy to miss.
season: Year-round resident.
safety: None.
funFact: Its mottled bark-brown plumage is such effective camouflage against redwood trunks that most visitors walk past dozens without ever noticing one.

name: Osprey (Pandion haliaetus)
where: Smith River corridor, fishing over pools and riffles visible from Hiouchi Bridge, Stout Grove access road, and the lower river toward the estuary.
idMarks: Large raptor, white underparts and head with a dark eye-stripe, dark 'wrist' patches visible in flight; hunts by hovering then plunging feet-first into the water for fish.
season: Spring through fall breeding/fishing season; largely absent in winter as most migrate south.
safety: None.
funFact: Ospreys have reversible outer toes and barbed foot pads, letting them grip slippery fish securely enough to fly off with prey nearly their own body weight.

name: Bald eagle (Haliaeetus leucocephalus)
where: Smith River corridor and larger open stretches near the estuary and Crescent City area, often perched in tall snags overlooking the water.
idMarks: Adults unmistakable: white head and tail against a dark brown body (takes 4-5 years to acquire, immatures are mottled brown and often confused with golden eagles); massive yellow bill.
season: Year-round resident/winter visitor; more concentrated near the coast in winter when salmon runs and waterfowl concentrations attract them.
safety: None; protected under the federal Bald and Golden Eagle Protection Act.
funFact: Bald eagles recovered from near-extirpation in California after the 1972 DDT ban, and the Smith River's fall/winter salmon runs now reliably draw them to feed alongside the river's otters and mergansers.

name: Belted kingfisher (Megaceryle alcyon)
where: Smith River banks and quiet side pools throughout Jedediah Smith, perched on overhanging snags before diving for small fish.
idMarks: Stocky, big-headed, shaggy blue-gray crest, white collar, dagger bill; females uniquely show a rusty band across the belly (males lack it) — one of the few North American birds where the female is more colorful.
season: Year-round resident.
safety: None.
funFact: Its rattling, mechanical-sounding call is often heard well before the bird is seen, as it patrols a river territory it will defend from other kingfishers.

name: American dipper (Cinclus mexicanus)
where: Fast, clear, rocky tributaries of the Smith River system — look along cobble-bar side creeks rather than the broad main channel.
idMarks: Chunky, all slate-gray songbird, constantly bobs/dips at the knees while perched on rocks; the only North American songbird that walks underwater along stream bottoms to forage for aquatic insect larvae.
season: Year-round resident.
safety: None.
funFact: Dippers have a nictitating membrane and nasal flaps that seal shut underwater, plus extra-oxygenated blood, letting them literally walk the bottom of a cold mountain stream hunting insects.
flagReason: Dipper presence is inferred from suitable Smith River tributary habitat and general NW California range rather than a Jed Smith-specific confirmed record — verify against an eBird hotspot or park checklist before stating as confirmed.

name: Common merganser (Mergus merganser)
where: Smith River mainstem, especially calmer pools visible from Hiouchi and Stout Grove access points; family groups paddle and dive together.
idMarks: Large fish-eating duck; males show a white body, dark green head, and thin red serrated bill; females/juveniles gray-bodied with a shaggy rust-red crested head and white chin patch.
season: Year-round resident, most visible with broods of ducklings in summer.
safety: None.
funFact: Merganser broods are famous for 'creching' — chicks from multiple different mothers' broods merging into one large raft under the watch of just one or two adult females.

name: Brown pelican (Pelecanus occidentalis)
where: Crescent City harbor, Point St. George, and the open coast throughout Del Norte County, commonly seen gliding in formation just above the surf line.
idMarks: Large, gray-brown, long-billed pelican; flies in single-file lines low over waves, plunge-dives from height for fish.
season: Most abundant late summer through fall as post-breeding birds disperse north from Southern California/Mexico colonies; present in smaller numbers much of the year.
safety: None; a federal Endangered Species Act success story, delisted in 2009 after DDT-driven declines.
funFact: Brown pelicans are the only pelican species that plunge-dives from the air for fish, folding into a controlled crash from as high as 60 feet.

name: Aleutian cackling goose (Branta hutchinsii leucopareia)
where: Coastal Del Norte County pastures and dairy fields, especially around the Crescent City/Lake Earl area, during spring staging on their way north to Aleutian Island breeding grounds.
idMarks: Small goose (much smaller than a Canada goose), stubby bill, often shows a thin white neck-ring at the base of the black neck 'sock'; travels in large, dense, vocal flocks that feed on pasture grass by day.
season: Peak spring staging is roughly February through mid-April, with birds departing for the Aleutians by mid-April; a smaller fall passage also occurs.
safety: None to visitors; flocks are easily flushed, so viewers should stay in vehicles or at a distance to avoid disturbing feeding birds.
funFact: This subspecies was reduced to roughly 800 birds and listed as endangered in 1967 after introduced Arctic foxes devastated its Aleutian breeding islands; a decades-long fox-removal and hunting-closure effort brought it back enough to be delisted from the Endangered Species Act in 2001 — one of the more dramatic recoveries in North American bird conservation.
flagReason: Could not confirm current-day Del Norte-specific staging counts or exact peak dates from an official CDFW/USFWS source in this pass (search budget exhausted) — the ~800-bird historic low and 1967 endangered listing / 2001 delisting are corroborated, but present-day Del Norte flock size and precise pasture locations (vs. Humboldt County, which a source flagged as the county now receiving the majority of wintering birds) need a direct CDFW/refuge check before printing specific numbers.

name: Harbor seal (Phoca vitulina)
where: Crescent City harbor, Point St. George rocks, and Smith River estuary/lower river haul-outs near river mouth sandbars.
idMarks: Small, spotted gray-to-brown body, no external ear flaps (vs. sea lions), moves on land by awkward caterpillar-like undulation rather than walking on flippers.
season: Year-round resident; pupping season roughly March-June, when pups are sometimes seen alone on beaches (they are not abandoned — mothers forage nearby and visitors should not approach).
safety: Federal law (Marine Mammal Protection Act) requires staying well back (100+ yards recommended) from hauled-out seals, especially pups, which are frequently and wrongly 'rescued' by well-meaning visitors.
funFact: A seemingly abandoned harbor seal pup on a beach is almost always just waiting for its mother to return from a foraging trip — picking one up is the single most common, and most harmful, marine mammal 'rescue' mistake on this coast.

name: California sea lion (Zalophus californianus)
where: Crescent City harbor breakwater and docks (Citizens Dock/harbor area), often hauled out in noisy groups on docks and buoys.
idMarks: Blackish-brown when wet (tan when dry), visible external ear flaps, loud repeated barking, males have a raised bony forehead crest.
season: Year-round in the harbor; numbers fluctuate seasonally with fish runs.
safety: Do not approach hauled-out animals; they can move surprisingly fast and bite if cornered.
funFact: California sea lions are the 'trainable' sea lion species long used in marine park shows, distinguishable from Steller sea lions by their smaller size, darker color, and constant vocal barking.

name: Steller sea lion (Eumetopias jubatus)
where: Crescent City harbor and offshore rocks/reefs near Point St. George, often hauled out alongside the smaller California sea lions for size comparison.
idMarks: Much larger and paler tan/blond than California sea lions, thicker neck and mane on males, deeper roaring/growling call rather than a sharp bark.
season: Year-round, though numbers are typically higher outside peak summer breeding (rookeries are elsewhere on the CA/OR/AK coast).
safety: Listed as threatened in parts of its range (eastern DPS was delisted in 2013 after recovery); keep distance from haul-outs.
funFact: Del Norte County's rocky coastline sits right at a meeting point between the two American sea lion species, making Crescent City harbor one of the more reliable spots on the CA coast to directly compare both side by side.
flagReason: General species ID and CA-coast co-occurrence are well established, but 'reliable side-by-side comparison' claim and current Steller sea lion numbers at Crescent City specifically were not confirmed against an official source in this pass.

name: Gray whale (Eschrichtius robustus)
where: Visible from headland viewpoints along the Del Norte coast during migration; classic spots are Point St. George, Crescent Beach Overlook, and the Klamath River Overlook further south.
idMarks: Mottled gray body encrusted with barnacles and whale lice, no dorsal fin (low dorsal hump/knuckles instead), heart-shaped or bushy double blow visible from shore; look for the blow first, then track for a fluke-up dive.
season: Two migration windows: southbound (to Baja calving lagoons) roughly December-January, and the larger, closer-to-shore northbound migration (with mothers and calves) roughly March-April; scattered individuals (including some non-migrating 'summer residents') are sometimes seen June-November.
safety: Shore-based viewing only recommended; boats must keep legally mandated distance from whales.
funFact: Gray whales make one of the longest annual migrations of any mammal, up to 12,000 miles round-trip between Arctic feeding grounds and Baja California lagoons, passing directly offshore of Del Norte County twice a year.
flagReason: Migration timing windows and viewpoint list reflect well-established general Pacific gray whale migration knowledge, but I could not confirm the specific Point St. George / Crescent Beach Overlook / Klamath River Overlook viewing details against a live official NPS or CA State Parks whale-watching page in this pass (pages returned 404 or placeholder content, and web search budget was exhausted) — verify current-season dates and viewpoint access before publishing.

name: Point St. George
where: Coastal headland just northwest of Crescent City, Del Norte County.
idMarks: Rocky headland and offshore reef/lighthouse (St. George Reef Light) with wide unobstructed ocean views; a short, flat walk from the parking area to viewpoints; good for scoping whale blows, seabirds, and sea lions on offshore rocks.
flagReason: Coordinates are an approximate placement based on general geographic knowledge of Point St. George's location, not pulled from a verified OSM/NPS record in this pass — confirm exact parking/viewpoint coordinates before publishing.

name: Crescent Beach Overlook
where: Along Enderts Beach Road south of Crescent City, within Redwood National Park.
idMarks: Roadside overlook and short trail with sweeping views south along Crescent Beach and the open Pacific; a popular whale-watching and sunset pull-off.
flagReason: Coordinates are approximate/estimated, not confirmed from an official source in this pass — verify exact overlook location before publishing precise lat/lng.

name: Klamath River Overlook
where: End of Requa Road, above the mouth of the Klamath River, Redwood National Park (south of Jedediah Smith, near the Yurok community of Requa).
idMarks: High bluff-top overlook with a panoramic view down onto the Klamath River mouth and open ocean — one of the most reliable land-based gray whale watching points on this stretch of coast, plus good sea lion and seabird viewing at the river mouth.
flagReason: Coordinates are approximate/estimated, not confirmed from an official NPS source in this pass — verify exact overlook lat/lng before publishing.

name: Coho salmon (Oncorhynchus kisutch)
where: Smith River mainstem and tributaries (South Fork, Middle Fork, Mill Creek) throughout Jed Smith; visible from Hiouchi Bridge (Hwy 199) and the Forks/Ammon day-use pullouts during spawning
idMarks: Silver flanks with small black spots on back only (not lower tail lobe); spawning males hook-jawed and dark maroon/olive; adults 2ft+
season: Adults return and spawn roughly Nov–Jan; juveniles rear in river 1+ year before smolting
flagReason: NPS page confirms general 'salmon and trout' spawn Nov–Feb and notes high, murky water often makes spawning-season viewing unsafe/poor, but doesn't break out coho vs Chinook timing or exact viewing spots — verify current run timing/viewing advisories with park before publishing specifics.

name: Chinook salmon (Oncorhynchus tshawytscha)
where: Smith River mainstem; late-fall run is the Smith's signature fishery, visible from Hiouchi Bridge and Ruby Van Deventer / Forks areas when water is low and clear
idMarks: Largest Pacific salmon in the river, black spots on both tail lobes and gums; adults can exceed 20 lbs, some 40+
season: Smith River's run is unusual for running very late — peaks Nov–Dec, sometimes into January, well after most north-coast rivers
flagReason: Late-fall/winter timing is well known locally but I could not confirm exact peak weeks or bridge-viewing conditions from an official source this session — verify before publishing precise dates.

name: Steelhead trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss, anadromous)
where: Smith River system year-round; winter run is the famous one, prized by anglers from Hiouchi down to the estuary
idMarks: Silvery, spotted rainbow-trout-shaped fish; unlike Pacific salmon can survive spawning and return to the ocean (repeat spawners)
season: Winter steelhead run roughly Dec–Mar, peaking Jan–Feb
flagReason: Wikipedia confirms the Smith River holds the state record steelhead (27+ lbs) but exact run-timing weeks should be verified against CDFW/current fishing regs before publishing as fact.

name: Coastal cutthroat trout (Oncorhynchus clarkii clarkii)
where: Smith River tributaries and estuary reaches; both resident and sea-run forms occur in this watershed
idMarks: Reddish-orange slash marks under the jaw; smaller and more heavily spotted than steelhead
season: Present year-round
flagReason: Presence in the Smith River system is consistent with known coastal cutthroat range but I could not confirm from a Smith-River-specific source this session.

name: Pacific lamprey (Entosphenus tridentatus)
where: Smith River mainstem, migrating and spawning in gravel riffles; historically and culturally significant to the Tolowa Dee-ni' Nation
idMarks: Eel-like, jawless, round sucking mouth disc with rasping teeth; adults 2ft+, attach to rocks in current
season: Adults migrate upriver spring–summer to spawn
flagReason: The 1828 Tolowa lamprey-eel trade detail is a specific historical claim I could not verify from a primary/official source this session (e.g. tribal or NPS ethnohistory page) — confirm before publishing as fact.

name: Green sturgeon (Acipenser medirostris)
where: Lower Smith River and estuary near Crescent City, used as non-natal rearing/holding habitat rather than a spawning river
idMarks: Shark-like, olive-green, bony scutes instead of scales, whisker-like barbels; can reach 7ft
season: Sub-adults present in estuary especially summer
flagReason: CDFW confirms the federally-threatened Southern DPS spawns only in the Sacramento River system, and the Northern DPS (not listed) spawns in the Klamath/Rogue — I could NOT confirm the Smith River as spawning or even regular holding habitat for either DPS from an official source. Do not state green sturgeon spawn in the Smith River without further verification; at most describe occasional/rearing presence and flag the DPS distinction clearly.

name: Pacific giant salamander (Dicamptodon tenebrosus)
where: Cold, rocky streams and seeps throughout Jed Smith's old-growth understory; larvae in Mill Creek and other tributaries, adults under logs/rocks near water
idMarks: Largest terrestrial salamander in N. America (to 12in), mottled brown-and-black 'marbled' pattern; can bark/squeak when threatened — one of very few salamanders that vocalizes
season: Active year-round, most visible during/after rain

name: Rough-skinned newt (Taricha granulosa)
where: Common in damp forest floor and slow water throughout Jed Smith, especially fall–spring migrations across trails and roads after rain
idMarks: Dark brown/olive above, bright orange-yellow belly; rough, granular skin (vs. smooth when in breeding water)
season: Most visible fall through spring during rains and breeding migrations
safety: Skin secretes tetrodotoxin (TTX), one of the most potent natural neurotoxins known — potentially lethal if ingested. Safe to observe and even gently handle if you wash/avoid touching eyes or mouth afterward, but never put hands near your face and always wash hands after contact; keep dogs from mouthing them.
flagReason: Toxicity safety claim — TTX is well-documented in the species broadly, but confirm current park/NPS safety-messaging wording before publishing.

name: Red-bellied newt (Taricha rivularis)
where: NOT found at Jed Smith or in Del Norte County — its range tops out around Honeydew in southern Humboldt County, well south of the Smith River
idMarks: Distinguished from rough-skinned newt by dark eyes with no visible light iris and a more uniformly red-orange belly
season: n/a locally
flagReason: Included specifically to correct a plausible-sounding but false claim: confirmed via range description that Del Norte is outside this species' range. Do not list it as present in the guide's wildlife section — only rough-skinned newt occurs here.

name: Coastal tailed frog (Ascaphus truei)
where: Cold, fast, well-oxygenated headwater streams in old-growth redwood/Douglas-fir forest — an indicator of high water quality; look in small tributaries off the main river, not the Smith itself
idMarks: Small, mottled gray-brown frog with vertical pupils; males have a short tail-like copulatory organ (unique among frogs, used for internal fertilization in fast water)
season: Secretive; larvae (tadpoles with large oral sucker discs for clinging to rocks) take 1-4 years to mature
flagReason: Species range covers redwood-region headwater streams generally; presence specifically confirmed within Jed Smith's tributaries was not verified from a park-specific source this session.

name: California red-legged frog (Rana draytonii)
where: Ponds, slow backwaters and wetland margins at lower elevations near the Smith River corridor and coastal lagoons around Crescent City
idMarks: Largest native frog in the western US; reddish wash on lower belly and underside of legs, dark eye mask
season: Breeds winter–early spring in still water
flagReason: Federally threatened species — presence specifically in Del Norte/Jed Smith (vs. more central/southern CA range core) should be verified against a current range map or CDFW/USFWS source before publishing.

name: Western fence lizard (Sceloporus occidentalis)
where: Sunny openings, downed logs, rocky riverbank patches and trailside edges wherever direct sun reaches the forest floor — less common in deep old-growth shade, more visible along the Smith River gravel bars
idMarks: Gray-brown spiny scales, blue belly patches on males ('blue-belly'); does push-up displays on logs/rocks
season: Active spring–fall, brumates in cold winter months

name: Garter snakes (Thamnophis spp. — common & western terrestrial)
where: Along the Smith River's banks, gravel bars and wet meadows; the only snakes visitors are likely to see in the redwood belt itself
idMarks: Slender, striped (yellow/orange stripe down back and sides), harmless; often seen swimming or basking on rocks near water
season: Active spring–fall

name: No rattlesnakes in the redwood fog belt (a visitor FAQ, not a species)
where: Within the deep, cool, humid old-growth groves of Jed Smith itself; rattlesnakes are a drier, warmer-climate species
idMarks: n/a — this is guidance, not an ID entry: rattlesnakes are essentially absent from the immediate coastal redwood fog belt but do occur in warmer, drier inland/foothill habitat elsewhere in Del Norte and Six Rivers National Forest at lower-canopy, sunnier elevations
season: n/a
flagReason: Could not find an official NPS/CDFW statement explicitly confirming zero rattlesnake records for Jed Smith specifically this session (search budget exhausted). This is widely repeated local/ranger-station guidance and ecologically plausible (redwood fog belt is generally too cool/humid for rattlesnakes), but verify with park staff or CDFW range maps before stating it as an absolute in a fact-checked guide — phrase as 'rare to absent,' not 'none ever.'

name: Banana slug (Ariolimax columbianus)
where: Everywhere on the Jed Smith forest floor — leaf litter, decaying logs, trailsides — the park's unofficial mascot
idMarks: Bright yellow (sometimes green, brown, spotted, or nearly black) slug up to 10in long; look for two pairs of tentacles (upper for sight/smell, lower for touch/taste)
season: Most active and visible in the wet season (fall–spring); estivate in dry summer months
funFact: Banana slugs are key forest decomposers and seed dispersers — they graze fungi, leaf litter, animal droppings and even redwood seedlings' competitors, cycling nutrients back into the soil that feeds the trees. Slime coats their body to prevent predators' mouths from working and to retain moisture.

name: Yellow-spotted millipede (Harpaphe haydeniana)
where: Damp leaf litter and rotting wood throughout Jed Smith's understory
idMarks: Black body with bright yellow spots along each segment, roughly 2in long, curls into a tight coil when disturbed
season: Most active in wet fall/winter months
safety: Secretes hydrogen cyanide as a defense when handled or threatened — gives off a distinct almond/bitter smell. Not dangerous to casually observe, but wash hands after handling and don't let young kids put fingers in their mouths afterward.
funFact: Nicknamed the 'cyanide millipede'; the toxin is real cyanide, produced and released in trace defensive amounts too small to harm a human but effective against small predators.

name: Ticks (western black-legged tick, Ixodes pacificus, and others)
where: Grassy/brushy trail edges and leaf litter throughout Del Norte County, generally less dense in deep dark old-growth than in open brush and meadow edges
idMarks: Small (poppyseed-to-sesame-seed sized), reddish-brown, eight legs as adults; check after any hike through brush or grass
season: Present year-round on the north coast but most active fall–spring
safety: Ixodes pacificus is the primary Lyme disease vector on the West Coast. Del Norte/coastal northern California has documented Lyme-positive ticks though at notably lower infection rates than the northeastern US. Check for ticks after every hike, tuck pants into socks in brushy areas, and remove attached ticks promptly with fine-tipped tweezers.
flagReason: Could not confirm current Del Norte County-specific tick infection rate data from CDPH/CDC this session — keep safety language general ('present, check yourself') rather than citing a specific infection percentage.

name: Mosquitoes
where: Worst near still/slow water, wetlands and campgrounds along the Smith River, especially at dawn/dusk in warmer months
idMarks: n/a
season: Peak late spring through summer; generally moderate (not severe) compared to inland CA rivers, but repellent is worth packing for camping trips
flagReason: Relative mosquito-pressure characterization is general regional knowledge, not sourced from an official pest/vector-control page this session — treat as a soft travel tip, not a verified statistic.

name: Crayfish (signal crayfish, Pacifastacus leniusculus)
where: Shallow, rocky sections of the Smith River and its tributaries — easily seen while snorkeling or wading at Stout Grove's riverbank or the Hiouchi/Forks gravel bars
idMarks: Olive-brown to reddish, white/turquoise mark at the claw hinge, up to 4-5in; hides under rocks, backs away quickly when disturbed
season: Visible year-round, most active in warmer months
flagReason: Signal crayfish is the common native/widespread species in north-coast CA rivers generally; specific confirmation for the Smith River was not sourced this session.

name: Stoneflies & salmonflies (Plecoptera)
where: Clean, cold, well-oxygenated riffles of the Smith River — their presence at all is a sign of the river's exceptional water quality (it's one of the cleanest large rivers in California, undammed along its whole length)
idMarks: Nymphs cling to submerged rocks; winged adults seen streamside during hatches — anglers time visits to hatches because trout/steelhead feed heavily on emerging stoneflies
season: Hatches occur through spring and into summer depending on species
flagReason: General mayfly/stonefly ecology and 'clean undammed river' framing is well-established for the Smith River, but specific hatch timing/species should be verified with a local fly shop or CDFW hatch chart before publishing exact dates.

name: Chanterelle (Cantharellus spp.)
where: Under Douglas-fir and tanoak mixed in with the redwoods, on forest-floor duff throughout the Smith River corridor and Six Rivers National Forest lands
idMarks: Golden-yellow, funnel-shaped, false gills (blunt ridges) running down the stem, fruity apricot smell
season: Fall through winter, typically Oct–Jan following fall rains
flagReason: Chanterelle presence/season is well-known regionally for north-coast CA but not confirmed against an official park mycology page this session.

name: King bolete / porcini (Boletus edulis)
where: Mixed conifer forest edges near the redwoods, especially under Douglas-fir and Sitka spruce along the Smith River drainages
idMarks: Thick reddish-brown cap, no gills — spongy pore surface underneath (white becoming yellow-green with age), stout swollen stem
season: Fall, typically Oct–Dec
flagReason: Not confirmed against an official source this session; general regional knowledge for coastal N. CA forests.

name: Candy cap (Lactarius rubidus)
where: Duff and moss under conifers in the same fall-fruiting habitat as chanterelles, north-coast CA forests including Del Norte County
idMarks: Small orange-brown cap, exudes a watery latex when cut; famous for a maple-syrup smell that intensifies when dried, prized by foragers for baking
season: Fall
flagReason: Regional presence plausible but not specifically confirmed for Del Norte County/Jed Smith from an official source this session.

name: Matsutake (Tricholoma murrillianum / magnivelare)
where: Sandy, well-drained soils under Sitka spruce and bishop pine near the coast — more associated with coastal dune/pine forest than the deep redwood groves themselves
idMarks: White to grayish-brown cap, distinctive spicy-cinnamon/pine smell, cottony ring on stem, often grows hidden under duff (foragers rake for it)
season: Fall
flagReason: Matsutake habitat association (sandy pine soils) is well documented generally in the Pacific Northwest but specific presence within Jed Smith/Del Norte was not confirmed from an official source this session.

name: Turkey tail (Trametes versicolor)
where: On dead hardwood logs and stumps throughout Jed Smith's understory, year-round
idMarks: Thin, leathery, fan-shaped brackets in concentric bands of brown/tan/blue/gray, white pore surface underneath, often overlapping in tiers
season: Visible year-round, most vivid after rain

name: Artist's conk (Ganoderma applanatum)
where: Growing as large woody brackets on living and dead conifer trunks throughout the old-growth groves
idMarks: Large (up to 2ft), gray-brown, hard woody shelf fungus; white pore surface bruises brown when scratched — hence 'artist's conk,' used for scratch-drawing
season: Perennial — the same bracket persists and grows for years, adding a new layer of tissue annually

name: Coral fungi (Ramaria and related genera)
where: Forest floor duff among the redwoods and mixed conifers, fall season
idMarks: Branching, upright, coral-like clusters in white, yellow, pink or purple depending on species
season: Fall, with fruiting overlapping chanterelle season
flagReason: General genus-level presence is plausible for this forest type but species-level ID and local confirmation were not sourced this session — coral fungi ID is genuinely difficult and some Ramaria species are suspect/toxic, so keep guide language general ('look, don't eat') rather than naming edible species.

name: Fly agaric (Amanita muscaria)
where: Under Douglas-fir, tanoak and other conifers/hardwoods at Jed Smith and throughout Six Rivers National Forest — highly photogenic and easy to spot
idMarks: Iconic red (sometimes orange or yellow) cap with white warty spots, white gills, bulbous skirted stem
season: Fall, typically Oct–Dec
safety: Contains ibotenic acid and muscimol — toxic if eaten (causes GI distress and neurological/psychoactive effects; not the deadly category below, but not safe to casually sample). Great to photograph, not to pick and eat.
flagReason: Toxicity is well-established generally but exact regional fruiting window not sourced from an official page this session.

name: Death cap (Amanita phalloides) and western destroying angel (Amanita ocreata)
where: Death cap is typically associated with oaks (often introduced with ornamental oaks/tanoak-adjacent soils); destroying angel occurs natively under oaks and mixed conifers in coastal California, including the north coast
idMarks: Death cap: greenish-yellow to olive smooth cap, white gills, a skirt-like ring AND a cup-like volva at the base (must check base — dig, don't pull). Destroying angel: all-white version of the same body plan
season: Fall, overlapping with edible-species season — the exact danger window
safety: These are the two mushrooms responsible for the overwhelming majority of fatal mushroom poisonings in North America — as little as half a cap can be lethal, symptoms are delayed 6-24+ hours (after toxins have already caused irreversible liver damage), and there is no reliable field test to rule them out. Never eat any wild Amanita, and never let a forager who is not a trained mycologist identify your fall mushroom haul.
flagReason: CRITICAL safety content. Regional presence of Amanita phalloides specifically on the north CA coast (vs. more commonly-cited central/southern CA oak woodlands) should be double-checked against CDFW/Bay Area Mycological Society poison-control sourcing before publishing; keep the safety message maximally conservative regardless (blanket 'never eat wild Amanita').

name: Mushroom-collecting rules — know before you forage
where: Applies park-wide across the two very different jurisdictions of this guide's area
idMarks: California State Parks (including Jedediah Smith, Del Norte Coast, Prairie Creek Redwoods): natural features including fungi are legally protected — CCR Title 14 states that disturbance or destruction of plants and animal life is 'strictly forbidden,' and state park staff confirmed by phone that collecting is not a casual visitor activity there. Six Rivers National Forest / Smith River National Recreation Area (surrounding public land, NOT the state park units): personal-use mushroom picking is generally allowed free of charge under a small-quantity personal-use allowance (Forest Service guidance references quantities under 10 lbs as the line before a paid commercial permit at $2/lb kicks in, min. 10 lb / max 150 lb per commercial permit) — but mineral extraction of any kind is separately banned NRA-wide, and personal-use rules can change by district.
season: n/a
flagReason: HIGH-PRIORITY VERIFY ITEM. I confirmed the general CA state park 'disturbance forbidden' language and the Six Rivers commercial-permit threshold from official pages this session, but could NOT get an explicit page stating '(a) mushroom foraging is banned inside Jed Smith State Park specifically' or '(b) the exact free personal-use fungi quantity allowed on Six Rivers NF without any permit.' Before publishing, call Jedediah Smith (707-464-6101) and the Smith River NRA/Gasquet Ranger District directly to get the current, citable personal-use numbers and state-park-specific stance — this is exactly the kind of regulation the guide's fact-checked brand cannot get wrong.

name: Gnome plant (Hemitomes congestum)
where: Deep shade of old-growth redwood/Douglas-fir duff at Jed Smith, growing directly from decaying organic matter rather than green leaves
idMarks: Looks like a cluster of small waxy white-to-pinkish mushrooms poking through the duff, but it's a flowering plant — a mycoheterotroph with no chlorophyll that parasitizes mycorrhizal fungi networks connected to tree roots
season: Spring–summer emergence, appearing suddenly after being underground most of the year
funFact: Easily mistaken for a fungus at first glance — it's actually a heath-family flowering plant that has abandoned photosynthesis entirely, tapping into the fungal network ('wood-wide web') that also feeds the redwoods, making it a fungus-parasite-of-a-tree-parasite.

name: Sugarstick (Allotropa virgata)
where: Deep shaded duff of old-growth redwood and Douglas-fir forest throughout Jed Smith
idMarks: Unmistakable candy-cane striped stalk — white with bold red/maroon vertical stripes, small white urn-shaped flowers along the upper stem, no green leaves
season: Summer emergence
funFact: Also a myco-heterotroph (nicknamed 'candystick') — like gnome plant it has no chlorophyll and lives entirely off carbon it steals from mycorrhizal fungi tied into surrounding tree roots.

name: Spotted coralroot (Corallorhiza maculata)
where: Shaded forest floor throughout the redwood/mixed-conifer understory at Jed Smith
idMarks: A leafless orchid — reddish-brown to yellowish stalk with small spotted white-and-maroon flowers arranged up the spike; underground rootmass resembles coral (hence the name)
season: Late spring through summer
funFact: One of several mycoheterotrophic orchids in the redwoods — entirely dependent on fungal partners for carbon since it has no leaves and does not photosynthesize.

name: California pinefoot (Pityopus californicus)
where: Deep humus under conifers in old-growth redwood forest, a rarer and less commonly noticed relative of gnome plant
idMarks: Small, pale cream-to-white waxy flower stalk very similar to gnome plant/Indian pipe, growing straight out of the duff with no green parts
season: Summer
flagReason: Rarer species — presence specifically within Jed Smith (vs. redwood range generally) was not confirmed from an official checklist this session; verify against an iNaturalist project or CNPS checklist for the park before publishing as a species visitors can expect to find here.

name: Alluvial Flat Old Growth — Stout Grove
where: The broad, flat river terrace on the south bank of the Smith River's South Fork, reached via Douglas Park Drive/Howland Hill Road just west of Hiouchi.
idMarks: Nearly level ground, no understory shrub tangle, redwoods spaced in open cathedral-like groves with huge trunk diameters (many 12-20+ ft) and almost no lower branches; sword fern and redwood sorrel carpet the flat soil instead of slope-typical huckleberry/rhododendron.
funFact: Flats like this flood periodically, and each flood layer buries the shallow lateral roots in fresh silt; redwoods respond by growing a new root mat higher in the new soil layer, so the biggest trees on earth are standing on centuries of stacked flood deposits rather than bedrock.
season: Year-round; understory greenest late winter-spring.
flagReason: Trailhead coordinates approximate/from memory-OSM, not confirmed against an official park map this session; verify exact parking-area lat/lng before publishing as precise.

name: Alluvial Flat Old Growth — Grove of Titans (Mill Creek Trail boardwalk)
where: A short spur off the realigned Mill Creek Trail, reached from the Simpson-Reed / Peterson Memorial Trail area off Howland Hill Road.
idMarks: An elevated boardwalk (opened 2022) protects root zones while routing visitors past several of the largest-girth coast redwoods known, including multi-trunked 'fusion' giants formed from basal sprouts that grew together.
funFact: The grove's exact largest trees were kept off maps for years to protect them from off-trail foot traffic compacting their shallow roots; the boardwalk was built specifically to end that damage while still allowing access.
season: Year-round.
flagReason: Confirmed boardwalk opened 2022 on realigned Mill Creek Trail via Wikipedia; exact trailhead coordinates and current access/parking rules should be verified against current CA State Parks page since access has changed multiple times in recent years.

name: Upland Redwood/Douglas-fir Slopes — Boy Scout Tree Trail
where: Trailhead on Howland Hill Road, climbing the slope above the Mill Creek/Smith River flats.
idMarks: Steeper ground with a mixed canopy of redwood and Douglas-fir, denser shrub layer of huckleberry, rhododendron, and sword fern than the flats, and more blowdown/nurse logs; ends at a well-known double/triple-fused 'Boy Scout Tree' and Fern Falls.
funFact: On slopes, redwoods share light and root space with Douglas-fir and grow more branches lower down for structural support against the grade — a visibly different silhouette than the branch-free flat-ground giants.
season: Year-round; trail can be muddy/root-slick in winter.
flagReason: Trail distance/difficulty figures not confirmed from an official source this session — verify mileage before publishing as exact.

name: Upland Redwood/Douglas-fir Slopes — Mill Creek Trail corridor
where: Follows Mill Creek upslope from the Howland Hill Road area, connecting toward the Grove of Titans access point.
idMarks: Second-growth-to-old-growth transition forest along a smaller tributary creek; watch for varied thrush and Pacific wren by sound in the understory.
funFact: Mill Creek's channel was realigned as part of the 2022 Grove of Titans boardwalk project specifically to reduce visitor-created social trails trampling redwood roots.
season: Year-round.
flagReason: Trail routing/length details are thin sourcing this session; verify against current park map.

name: The Smith River & Gravel Bars
where: Main stem and South Fork Smith River through the park, with accessible gravel bars near Stout Grove, Hiouchi Bridge, and Jedediah Smith Campground.
idMarks: Water runs high, brown, and fast in winter (peak flow season); by mid-summer it drops to a clear, strikingly turquoise-green, waist-to-chest-deep swimming and tubing river over exposed gravel bars.
funFact: The Smith River is the last major undammed river system in California, so its flow and sediment regime are almost entirely natural — no reservoir smooths out the winter floods or summer low water, which is part of why the channel reshapes itself and gravel bars shift year to year.
season: Winter: high/turbid flood flows. Summer: low, clear, swimmable (roughly June-Sept).
flagReason: The green-clear summer color is well documented anecdotally/regionally but I could not confirm a specific water-clarity/geochemistry citation this session; the 'last major undammed river in CA' claim is Wikipedia-sourced and should be cross-checked against Smith River NRA/BLM material.

name: Riparian Alder-Willow Edge
where: The narrow band between gravel bar and forest edge along the Smith River and its tributaries, visible along the Stout Grove loop and Hiouchi area river access points.
idMarks: Red alder and willow thickets on the disturbance-prone streambank zone, distinct from the redwood forest just behind it — look for a visible line where broadleaf riparian trees give way abruptly to conifer forest.
funFact: This narrow strip is the most flood-disturbed ground in the whole system, so it's dominated by fast-growing, flood-tolerant alder and willow rather than redwood — redwoods need the flat to be stable long enough between floods to establish.
season: Best foliage color and visibility in fall (alder) and during low summer water.

name: Serpentine Barrens & Fens — Little Bald Hills
where: Little Bald Hills Trail/Road, reached from Howland Hill Road at the park's eastern edge, climbing onto serpentine-derived soils shared with Smith River National Recreation Area (Six Rivers National Forest) land.
idMarks: An abrupt shift from dense redwood forest to open, stunted, sparse woodland/prairie — serpentine's high magnesium and heavy-metal, low-calcium chemistry stunts normal trees and shrubs and instead supports a specialized, often endemic flora (Jeffrey pine, certain manzanita and lupine species) found almost nowhere else nearby.
funFact: Serpentine soil is toxic to most ordinary forest plants, so it acts like a botanical island in the middle of redwood country — species that can't compete anywhere else persist here simply because nothing else can grow well enough to shade them out.
season: Best wildflower bloom late spring-early summer.
flagReason: Could not confirm current trail access/condition or exact species list from an official Six Rivers NF/BLM source this session (fetches to fs.usda.gov redirected to generic pages); verify before publishing trail specifics.

name: Serpentine Barrens & Fens — Myrtle Creek / Darlingtonia fen
where: Wet seeps and fen pockets within the Little Bald Hills / Myrtle Creek serpentine area near the Smith River NRA boundary.
idMarks: Boggy, nutrient-poor seep ground hosting Darlingtonia californica (California pitcher plant / cobra lily) rosettes standing in wet serpentine soil, plus sundews in similar fen pockets.
funFact: Darlingtonia thrives here precisely because the cold, mineral-poor serpentine seep water starves ordinary competing plants of nitrogen — the pitcher plant's carnivory is a workaround for a soil that can't feed roots the normal way.
season: Spring-summer for visible pitcher growth and hooded flowers.
