flagReason: Exact fen location/trail access to this specific site not confirmed from an official source this session — treat as a known regional habitat type rather than a pinned, verified visitor site until checked against a Six Rivers NF or CNPS source.

name: Coastal Dunes & Lagoon — Tolowa Dunes State Park / Lake Earl Wildlife Area
where: North of Crescent City along the coast, encompassing Lake Earl and Lake Tolowa and their surrounding dune system.
idMarks: Open coastal dune scrub and grassland surrounding a large, shallow, periodically-breaching freshwater/brackish lagoon complex — a strong contrast to the dense forest a few miles inland; major waterfowl and shorebird concentrations, including wintering waterfowl and nesting western snowy plover in dune habitat.
funFact: Lake Earl and Lake Tolowa together form a roughly 6,100-acre wildlife area, and because a sandbar periodically opens and closes at the ocean, the lagoon swings between freshwater and brackish/estuarine conditions depending on when it last breached.
season: Fall-winter best for waterfowl and migratory shorebirds.
flagReason: The 6,100-acre figure for the combined Lake Earl Wildlife Area is confirmed via Wikipedia this session, but the common claim that it is 'the largest lagoon system on the California coast' could NOT be verified from any source I could reach this session — do not publish that superlative without checking a CDFW or CA State Parks source directly.

name: Rocky Shore & Tidepools — Pebble Beach / Point St. George
where: Along the coast just north/west of downtown Crescent City, off Pebble Beach Drive and Point St. George Road.
idMarks: Exposed rocky intertidal shelf and offshore sea stacks; low tide reveals tidepools with sea stars, anemones, chitons, and surfgrass beds — a wave-battered rocky-shore zonation very different from the sand-lagoon habitat just to the north.
funFact: Point St. George's offshore reef and Dragon Rocks are treacherous enough that they're the site of a historic shipwreck (the Brother Jonathan, 1865) — a reminder that the same rocky structure creating rich tidepool habitat also makes this one of the most hazardous stretches of the whole California coast for ships.
season: Best tidepooling on minus low tides, check a tide table; typically better access spring-summer daytime low tides.
flagReason: Could not confirm current official access rules, species checklist, or tide-timing specifics from CDFW/CA State Parks this session — verify before publishing as a definitive visitor guide entry.

name: Rocky Shore & Tidepools — Enderts Beach / Crescent Beach
where: South of Crescent City off Enderts Beach Road, within Redwood National Park.
idMarks: A short forested trail descends to a rocky cove and tidepool shelf at the north end of Crescent Beach — one of the most accessible tidepool stops in the whole park complex.
funFact: This stretch sits right at the boundary where redwood forest runs down almost to the tideline, so it's possible to walk from old-growth canopy to tidepools in well under a mile.
season: Low tide, ideally a minus tide.
flagReason: Trailhead distance/coordinates and current trail-access status not confirmed from an official NPS page this session (fetch attempt to the NPS Enderts Beach page 404'd) — verify before publishing precise trail stats.

name: Second-growth vs Old-growth — reading the difference
where: Comparison is best made along Howland Hill Road, where the road passes through both older second-growth stands (logged mid-20th century, now regrown) and adjacent untouched old growth within a few minutes' drive/walk of each other.
idMarks: Second growth: even-aged trunks of similar diameter standing in tight rows or 'fairy rings' (circles of trunks sprouted from one cut stump's root crown), thin canopy gaps, little large downed wood. Old growth: wildly uneven trunk diameters, huge fallen 'nurse logs', multi-layered canopy, standing snags, and charred fire-scar cavities ('goosepens') at the base of some trees.
funFact: A 'fairy ring' isn't a separate species growing in a circle — it's the same individual tree's root system throwing up a ring of clone sprouts around the stump after the original trunk was cut, so a tight circle of same-age redwoods is basically a logging scar you can still read a century later.
season: Year-round.

name: Stout Grove Trail
where: Jedediah Smith Redwoods SP, reached via Howland Hill Road (unpaved) or, in summer, via the seasonal footbridge from Hiouchi/Douglas Park Rd across the Smith River
idMarks: 0.5 mi loop, flat, easy, wheelchair/stroller-friendly gravel path through a grove of old-growth coast redwoods on the Smith River floodplain — arguably the single best 'wow' grove for the time invested
flagReason: Mileage (0.5 mi) matches long-standing park literature but could not re-confirm current CA State Parks trail page text this session (site returned no trail-specific detail on fetch); verify current signage.
season: Year-round; best in filtered morning light spring–fall
funFact: Stout Grove was the site of a 1962 visit by President Kennedy and has been used in Star Wars: Return of the Jedi (speeder-bike sequence footage nearby).

name: Simpson-Reed Discovery Trail / Peterson Memorial Trail
where: Off Howland Hill Road, ~1 mile east of the Hiouchi Road junction
idMarks: ~1 mi loop (combined Simpson-Reed + Peterson), easy, flat boardwalk-and-dirt loop through massive old-growth with heavy sorrel and fern understory — quieter than Stout Grove
season: Year-round
funFact: One of the few Jed Smith old-growth loops accessible without walking Howland Hill Road's narrow shoulder, since it starts right at a pullout.

name: Leiffer Loop / Ellsworth Loop Trail
where: Trailhead on Walker Road/Little Bald Hills Rd near park HQ, Hiouchi
idMarks: ~2 mi combined loop, easy-moderate, less-visited old-growth loop with a creek crossing; good for solitude
season: Year-round
funFact: Named for local families; one of the less-photographed groves so it rarely feels crowded even in July.

name: Hiouchi Trail
where: Follows the north bank of the Smith River from Hiouchi Bridge/Hwy 199 area upstream toward Stout Grove
idMarks: ~4 mi one-way (river's-edge old growth, some elevation), moderate; can be combined with Stout Grove for a longer river-view hike
flagReason: 4-mile figure is the commonly cited park mileage but not re-confirmed on an official page this session.
season: Spring–fall; river views best at low summer flow
funFact: Runs close enough to the Smith to see rafters and swimmers below the trail in summer.

name: Hatton Trail / Hatton Loop
where: Off Douglas Park Rd near the Jed Smith campground, connecting toward the summer footbridge
idMarks: Short loop (~0.5 mi) plus a longer ~4 mi option linking to Stout Grove via the seasonal footbridge; easy, family-friendly, near the campground amphitheater
flagReason: Access depends on the summer-only footbridge being installed (typically ~Memorial Day–Labor Day) — confirm current installation dates with the park before relying on this route.
season: Best when the summer footbridge is up (roughly late May–September)
funFact: The footbridge is removed each fall before the Smith River's winter high flows would destroy it, then rebuilt by park crews the following late spring.

name: Nickerson Ranch Trail
where: Little Bald Hills area, off Howland Hill/Little Bald Hills Road
idMarks: ~1 mi, easy-moderate, quiet mixed forest walk, good early/late-season option when higher trails are muddy
flagReason: Could not confirm current trailhead location/condition from an official source this session — verify at the visitor center before hiking.
season: Fall–spring

name: Mill Creek Trail
where: Trailhead off Howland Hill Road; now the official route to the Grove of Titans boardwalk
idMarks: ~5-6 mi round trip depending on start point (the realigned section to Grove of Titans is ~3 mi); moderate, well-graded old-growth walk along Mill Creek
season: Year-round; can be muddy Nov–Mar
funFact: The current trail and 1,300-ft elevated boardwalk (completed May 2022, ~$4M, 23,000+ volunteer/crew hours) were built specifically to stop visitors from bushwhacking to the Titans and trampling their shallow roots.

name: Boy Scout Tree Trail (to Fern Falls)
where: Trailhead on Howland Hill Road, roughly 2.5 miles from the Hiouchi end
idMarks: 5.5 mi round trip, moderate, rooty single-track through dense old growth ending at 15-ft Fern Falls; the Boy Scout Tree itself (a fused double redwood) is about 2.9 mi in
flagReason: Mileage matches long-standing park literature; confirm current trailhead parking (small unpaved pullout, fills early) conditions locally.
season: Best spring–fall; can be very muddy in winter
funFact: No official trail markers for the Boy Scout Tree itself — hikers watch for an unsigned spur near a large downed log.

name: Little Bald Hills Trail
where: East end of Howland Hill Road / Little Bald Hills Road, transitioning into Six Rivers National Forest
idMarks: ~10 mi round trip (out-and-back to the serpentine barrens and backcountry camp), moderate-strenuous, unique because it climbs out of redwoods onto open, stunted-forest serpentine soil with different wildflowers
flagReason: 10-mi figure is the commonly cited total but not re-confirmed on an official current page this session.
season: Late spring for wildflowers on the serpentine barrens; passable most of year
funFact: Serpentine soil is toxic to most plants, so this is one of the only spots in the park with sun-loving, drought-adapted, dwarfed vegetation instead of redwood shade.

name: Grove of Titans Boardwalk
where: Via the realigned Mill Creek Trail off Howland Hill Road, Jedediah Smith Redwoods SP
idMarks: Reached by a 3-mile trail section ending in a 1,300-ft elevated boardwalk; ADA-accessible parking and restrooms at the trailhead; home to some of the most massive-volume coast redwoods known, including the Titan itself
season: Year-round; go early or on a weekday to avoid the (now-controlled) crowds
funFact: The grove was 'secretly' known to researchers for years and only widely publicized after National Geographic covered it in 2011, which caused enough off-trail damage to trigger this $4M restoration project.

name: Howland Hill Road (scenic drive)
where: Connects Hiouchi (Hwy 199) to Crescent City side, running through the heart of Jed Smith's old growth
idMarks: ~6-mile unpaved, narrow, one-lane-in-places forest road through cathedral-like redwoods; no RVs or trailers, allow 30-45 min minimum, pull-outs required for oncoming traffic
flagReason: Could not confirm current road/closure status this session (web search budget was exhausted) — this road is subject to seasonal grading, storm damage, and occasional closures; call the Jed Smith Visitor Center or check CA State Parks alerts before driving, especially after winter storms.
season: Best April-October; can be rutted/muddy or closed after winter storms
funFact: Considered one of the most beautiful drives in California despite (because of) being unpaved.

name: Smith River Summer Footbridge
where: Crosses the Smith River near the Jed Smith campground, connecting to Stout Grove
idMarks: Seasonal pedestrian bridge, installed roughly late May–early September; lets hikers/bikers reach Stout Grove and River Beach without driving Howland Hill Road
flagReason: Exact install/removal dates vary by year with river flow — confirm current-season dates with the park before planning around it.
season: Summer only

name: River Beach / Jed Smith day-use swimming
where: Along the Smith River within Jedediah Smith Redwoods SP, near the campground and summer footbridge
idMarks: Gravel bar swimming holes with clear, cold, glacially blue-green water; no lifeguards; look for calmer side channels versus the main current
flagReason: No lifeguards and current strength varies with flow/season — flag as a safety item; check conditions and swim only in marked calm areas.
season: Mid-June through September for comfortable swimming temps
funFact: The Smith is California's longest remaining undammed river system, which is why the water runs so clear.

name: Battery Point Lighthouse
where: Small tidal island just off Crescent City's harbor, downtown
idMarks: Reached on foot across a sand/rock isthmus only at low tide — check tide tables before walking out, the crossing can flood quickly; 1852 lighthouse and keeper's museum run by the Del Norte Historical Society
flagReason: Tour season/hours (Apr–Sep daily 10-4, Oct–Mar weekends 10-4 per Wikipedia) and admission price could not be confirmed from the Historical Society's own site this session — verify current hours and fee before visiting.
season: Best at low tide, any season; museum has seasonal hours
funFact: It's a genuine tidal island — at high tide the lighthouse is completely cut off from the mainland, one of the few U.S. lighthouses you walk to across the ocean floor.

name: Crescent City Harbor sea lions
where: Crescent City Harbor, near B Street Pier and the small boat basin
idMarks: Free, year-round hangout spot; California sea lions haul out on the docks and breakwater, especially near the fish processing area — bring ear protection for the noise, no ticket needed
season: Year-round, largest numbers late summer-fall

name: Northcoast Marine Mammal Center
where: Crescent City Harbor, adjacent to the boat basin
idMarks: Small free (donation-based) nonprofit seal/sea lion rescue and rehab center with outdoor viewing pools of recovering pinnipeds; family-friendly, 20-30 min visit
flagReason: Could not confirm current hours/admission this session — check their site or call ahead, hours can be seasonal/volunteer-dependent.
season: Year-round
funFact: Volunteers hand-rear orphaned or stranded seal and sea lion pups found along the Del Norte coast.

name: B Street Pier
where: Downtown Crescent City waterfront
idMarks: Free public fishing pier and walk with harbor, sea lion, and sunset views; flat, easy, wheelchair accessible
season: Year-round

name: Beachfront Park & Kidtown
where: Along Front Street, Crescent City waterfront, near the harbor
idMarks: Free community-built wooden playground plus a sandy beach strip, picnic areas, and a small skate park; good rainy-day/kid-decompression stop
season: Year-round
funFact: Kidtown was built largely by community volunteers in the 1990s, castle-and-fort style.

name: Brother Jonathan Cemetery & Vista Point
where: Hilltop off 9th Street, Crescent City
idMarks: Free, short walk from parking; ocean-view bluff cemetery memorializing 1865 shipwreck victims (the steamship Brother Jonathan), with interpretive plaques and a sweeping coastal panorama
season: Year-round; sunset is popular
funFact: The Brother Jonathan sank in 1865 after hitting an uncharted rock, the worst shipwreck on the West Coast to that date; some victims are buried here and it's said to be the first mass disaster memorial funded partly by the U.S. government.

name: Point St. George
where: Northwest of Crescent City, end of Radio Road/Pebble Beach Drive area
idMarks: Free, easy bluff-top walk with wide grassy headlands, tidepools below, and views to St. George Reef Lighthouse offshore; excellent for whale watching (Dec-Jan southbound, Mar-Apr northbound gray whale migration) and wind
season: Winter/spring for gray whale migration; windy year-round, dress warm
funFact: St. George Reef Lighthouse, visible offshore, was one of the most expensive lighthouses ever built (1892) due to the treacherous reef it sits on, and is only reachable today by helicopter tour days run by a private preservation society.

name: Pebble Beach Drive
where: Coastal road connecting Crescent City to Point St. George / Radio Road
idMarks: Free scenic coastal drive, ~10-15 min, with pullouts for surf-watching, rock formations, and sunset views; no formal trail, just roadside stops
season: Year-round, especially sunset

name: Radio Road sunset spot
where: Bluff-top pullouts along Radio Road near Point St. George
idMarks: Free, informal roadside pullouts facing directly west/southwest — one of the most open, unobstructed sunset horizons on this stretch of coast
flagReason: Local-knowledge spot; could not confirm with an official source this session.
season: Year-round

name: Tolowa Dunes State Park / Lake Earl Wildlife Area
where: North of Crescent City, off Lake Earl Drive
idMarks: Free, extensive dune/lagoon system and California's largest coastal lagoon (Lake Earl/Lake Talawa); excellent birding (waterfowl, shorebirds, raptors), multiple trailheads, some sandy/muddy sections
flagReason: Specific trail mileages and current access points not re-confirmed from an official source this session — check the Tolowa Dunes docent program or CDFW Lake Earl Wildlife Area page for current trail conditions.
season: Fall-spring for migratory waterfowl
funFact: Lake Earl is a rare coastal lagoon that periodically breaches naturally to the ocean, changing its salinity and shoreline over time.

name: Crescent Beach Overlook & Enderts Beach tidepools
where: South of Crescent City off Enderts Beach Road, Redwood National Park
idMarks: Overlook is a short walk from a parking pullout; Enderts Beach itself is roughly 0.5-1 mi down a steeper access trail to reach tidepools at low tide
flagReason: Tidepooling safety and best-tide timing depend on the day's tide table — check NOAA tide predictions before going, and note tidepool life is protected (no collecting).
season: Low tide, any season; whale watching Dec-Apr from the overlook
funFact: This overlook is also a low-key gray whale watching spot during migration.

name: Damnation Creek Trail
where: Trailhead on old Highway 101 (Coastal Drive) south of Crescent City, Del Norte Coast Redwoods SP
